Guide

Vitamins and minerals

Vitamin D is a supplement decision from the first days. Iron is a food decision from six months. The rest follows the diet.

Findings

Breastfed infants need a vitamin D supplement. Food will not cover it. In Hungarian practice the usual prevention dose is prescribed by the paediatrician or health visitor, often 400 IU a day.
Iron comes from food after six months, not from a routine tonic. Meat, legumes, and fortified cereal are the sources. A supplement is for a diagnosed deficiency or a specific risk, not a default.
A vegan infant diet needs a plan, not optimism. Vitamin B12, iodine, iron, zinc, calcium, and DHA do not appear by accident in a plant-only diet.
Liver is a vitamin A dose. Once a week, in a small portion, is plenty. Do not add a vitamin A supplement on top.

Vitamin D

Infants in Central Europe do not make enough vitamin D from sun for most of the year, and breast milk contains little. The NHS recommends 8.5 to 10 micrograms (340 to 400 IU) a day for breastfed babies from birth to one year. Hungarian paediatric practice commonly prescribes a daily vitamin D drop in that neighbourhood, sometimes up to a higher prevention dose. Use the product and the dose you were given. Do not stack a second product ‘to be safe’.

Infant formula already contains vitamin D. A baby drinking around 500 ml or more a day may not need an extra drop; this is a question for the prescriber, because the right answer depends on the formula and the volume.

Iron, zinc, and iodine

The dietary iron need in the second six months is high relative to body size, about 11 mg a day in US reference values, and it is met by food frequency rather than by one heroic portion. Serve an iron food most days. Zinc travels with meat and with beans. Plants alone are a thinner zinc source.

Iodine matters for the thyroid and for development. Dairy, eggs, and fish carry it. Iodised salt is the population tool and is the wrong tool under one year, because salt itself is restricted. A breastfeeding mother’s iodine intake matters; that is her supplement conversation, not a reason to salt the baby.

Vegetarian and vegan plates

A lacto-ovo vegetarian infant diet can work if eggs and dairy are actually eaten and iron is planned. A vegan diet can be constructed and is easy to get wrong. ESPGHAN asks that vegan infants receive medical and dietetic supervision and a reliable vitamin B12 source. Iodine, DHA from an algal oil, iron, zinc, and calcium need named foods, not a hope that variety will cover them.

Plant drinks are not infant formula. Rice drinks are unsuitable under five. Other plant drinks are not a main drink in the first year unless a clinician has chosen a specific product.

Vitamin A and the liver rule

Liver is rich in iron and so rich in preformed vitamin A that a large or frequent portion can overshoot. A small serving, about 15 grams of cooked liver in the child’s share, at most once a week, is the cautious reading of that fact. Skip liver entirely in a week when a vitamin A containing supplement is being used.

Ordinary vegetables supply carotenoids, which the body converts in a regulated way. There is no matching limit on carrots. Orange skin from carrots is harmless and fades.
